channel.title: Worldview Weekly
channel.description: A weekly global counterweight reading feed: concise, analytical, low-noise, and deliberately broader in perspective than The Economist.

item.title: The Future, Made in China — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 10, 2026 issue · long (~40 min)

Evan Osnos reports from China on the cumulative payoff from decades of industrial policy, infrastructure, scientific investment, automation and increasingly capable AI. The piece takes Chinese technological strength seriously while also dwelling on the political control, demographic weakness, labor disruption and brittle state-society bargain beneath it. Its most useful conclusion is that the emerging order may be neither American nor Chinese but a less orderly world of hedging, subsidy and coercive leverage.

Counterweight: Complicates a market-efficiency account of China by showing where state capacity has produced real technological gains, while refusing the opposite mistake of treating those gains as proof that authoritarian control is a superior development model.

item.title: The End of the European Summer — The New Yorker
item.description:
The New Yorker · August 24, 2026 issue · long (~30–35 min)

Eric Klinenberg examines how Europe, warming at more than twice the global average, is redesigning cities for heat they were never built to withstand. Paris, Milan and other cities are experimenting with shade, vegetation, water, pedestrianization and cooling infrastructure as heat becomes a public-health, inequality and economic problem rather than an occasional weather event.

Counterweight: Shifts climate policy from carbon-price abstractions toward adaptation, urban public goods and distribution: who has shade, cooling, green space and the ability to escape dangerous heat.

item.title: Green Strategy in Africa — Phenomenal World
item.description:
Phenomenal World · August 13, 2026 · medium-long (~20 min)

Kate Mackenzie and Tim Sahay survey an African industrial strategy taking shape around cheap Chinese solar, critical minerals, local processing and selective export restrictions. Morocco’s manufacturing ascent, Guinea’s bauxite policy, Zimbabwe’s lithium processing and the DRC’s cobalt restrictions suggest governments are trying to capture more value rather than remain raw-material suppliers.

Counterweight: Treats green transition and industrial policy as development strategy, not merely emissions reduction, and takes seriously the bargaining power of commodity-producing states.

item.title: Peru’s So-Called Paradox — Phenomenal World
item.description:
Phenomenal World · August 15, 2026 · long (~30 min)

Stephan Gruber challenges the familiar story that Peru combines dysfunctional politics with exemplary macroeconomic technocracy. He argues that the two are connected: an extractive, foreign-investment-dependent growth regime has delivered monetary stability while reinforcing informality, regional inequality, weak productive diversification and recurring conflict over mining and land.

Counterweight: Questions the clean separation between sound macroeconomic management and democratic legitimacy, asking what apparent stability is for and who bears its structural costs.

item.title: The End of Neoliberalism — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · Summer 2026 · medium (~15 min)

Branko Milanovic argues that neoliberal globalization has not simply been defeated by its critics; its own political and social consequences helped destroy the coalition that sustained it. The successor is not a coherent post-neoliberal settlement but a mixture of protectionism, restrictions on migration and attempts to restore older social arrangements.

Counterweight: Useful against accounts that treat the retreat from globalization chiefly as policy error or populist irrationality; Milanovic emphasizes endogenous political consequences of the old model.

item.title: The End of Morality — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · Summer 2026 · medium (~12–15 min)

Rosa Brooks argues that the erosion of international law matters even when powerful states have always violated it. Shared legal language created expectations, focal points and constraints at the margins; losing that normative grammar makes behavior less legible and collective-action problems harder to manage.

Counterweight: Pushes against a purely realist dismissal of international law as hypocrisy. Even imperfect rules can be functional infrastructure for coordination.

item.title: Cement’s Stubborn Emissions — Phenomenal World
item.description:
Phenomenal World · August 19, 2026 · long (~25 min)

Jack Copley explains why cement decarbonization is stalled by political economy as much as chemistry. Chronic overcapacity, weak profitability, long-lived plants, debt discipline and absent green premiums discourage expensive investment even when technical pathways exist. Europe’s limited progress has depended heavily on public subsidy and managed market conditions.

Counterweight: Reframes decarbonization from a story of carbon prices and technological substitution into one about industrial structure, finance, excess capacity and public coordination.

item.title: AI Needs Public Feedback At Scale Before It’s Too Late — Noema
item.description:
Noema · August 14, 2026 · short-medium (~10 min)

Nathan Gardels argues that AI and networked media should be used not only to accelerate disruption but to build mechanisms for large-scale public feedback and social consensus. Earlier communications revolutions destabilized politics before societies developed institutions capable of absorbing them; AI may require deliberately constructing those feedback institutions much faster.

Counterweight: Moves AI governance beyond the usual innovation-versus-regulation frame toward democratic institution design and collective preference formation.

item.title: Doomsday Climate Scenarios Were Wrong. That Doesn’t Help Europe. — Foreign Policy
item.description:
Foreign Policy · June 30, 2026 · medium (~12 min)

Jason Bordoff and Noah Kaufman concede that climate advocacy leaned too heavily on extreme emissions scenarios, but argue that correcting those assumptions does not justify complacency. Europe is already warming rapidly, damages remain deeply uncertain, and energy-security shocks strengthen the case for electrification and domestic clean power.

Counterweight: A useful corrective in both directions: less apocalyptic than some climate advocacy, but more attentive to uncertainty, resilience and tail risk than a simple cost-benefit story.

item.title: The Strange Defeat of Nuclear Deterrence — Foreign Affairs
item.description:
Foreign Affairs · July/August 2026 · medium-long (~20 min)

Rose Gottemoeller argues that recent wars expose a paradox: nuclear arsenals still constrain direct great-power escalation, yet they do not reliably deter conventional, drone, cyber or hybrid attacks against nuclear-armed states. That gap can encourage proliferation without actually making conventional conflict less likely. She proposes extending taboos and reciprocal restraint around attacks on nuclear facilities.

Counterweight: Complicates both nuclear hawkishness and abolitionist simplicity by focusing on the increasingly porous boundary between strategic deterrence and ordinary warfare.
